text: Hi, I'm Saravana. This is a walkthrough of my Automation and QA Developer assessment for Oytra. It covers the QA report, the n8n morning-brief workflow, and the bonus uptime monitor. Everything is in the public GitHub repository linked at the end.

Task one. The demo URL in the brief, demo dot realworld dot i o, no longer exists, so I tested the official replacement, demo dot realworld dot show. I scripted every main flow in a real Chrome browser with Puppeteer: sign-up, login, create, edit, delete, and logout. I also probed the API directly with curl. The short version for a non-technical reader: the happy path works, and the broken feeling comes from edge cases nobody guarded against.

I found twelve issues: one critical, two high, five medium, and four low. Highlights: a one-character password is accepted, and there is no throttling on wrong login attempts. A missing article shows a blank page instead of a message. Login fails if you type your email with different capitalisation. And form fields have no labels for screen readers. I also recorded what passed: script injection is escaped properly, and double-clicking publish creates only one article.

For the root-cause analysis I picked the critical bug. A title made only of spaces passes the required check, because the server never trims it. The slug generator then turns it into an empty string. Every article route is keyed by slug, so the article can never be opened, edited, or deleted again. The fix: trim and validate input, fall back to a generated slug when it comes out empty, add a database constraint, mirror the rule in the Angular form, and add a regression test.

Task two is an n8n workflow I call the HackerNews Morning Brief. It starts from an hourly schedule or a webhook I can call with curl. The first HTTP request pulls the HackerNews front page from the Algolia API. A Code node keeps the top five stories by points. Then two calls to a second API, HackerNews Firebase, fetch the number one story and its top comment as the enrichment. An IF node checks whether the top story has more than three hundred points, and sends either a hot-day brief or a normal brief to Telegram.

Here is a successful execution. On the left is the enrichment response with the comment ids. On the right is the transformed digest: top points, title, and the formatted top-five list. The bot token is kept in n8n's credential store, and the exported JSON only references the credential by name.
And this is the message that arrived in Telegram from the bot.

Error handling. Every HTTP node retries three times, then sends its error output to a fallback branch that posts an alert instead of failing silently. To prove it, I blocked the Algolia hostname inside the n8n container and triggered the webhook. The execution took the green error path and sent the fallback alert. On top of that, a separate Error Trigger workflow is linked to both workflows and reports any unexpected crash.

The bonus task is an uptime monitor. Every five minutes, a Code node requests the app, with up to three attempts and response-time measurement. If the status isn't two hundred, it sends a down alert. If the app is up but slower than three seconds, it sends a slow warning. Each check is stored in workflow static data, and a daily nine A M trigger posts the uptime percentage, average and worst response time, and failure count.
The repository has the PDF report, the repro scripts, the three exported workflows, the screenshots, and a one-page README. Thanks for watching. I'm happy to walk through any decision in more detail.
